corrected_value.title: Responsiveness without Representation: Evidence from Minimum Wage Laws in U.S. States

decisions.quote:
We replicate and expand a recent study by Simonovits, Guess,

and Nagler (2019) to explore if its conclusion – a pronounced and uniform conservative

bias – has stood.
decisions.reason: Shipped row 814 and blind target 0 identify the same original study: Simonovits, Guess, and Nagler (published online in 2018 and in print in 2019 in American Journal of Political Science, DOI 10.1111/ajps.12412), which is the sole published study replicated in this paper. (Shipped row 428 was a duplicate row erroneously listing the OSF working-paper version of this replicating study itself, 10.31235/osf.io/3ye4b, and was paired with target 0 in prior adjudication.)

decisions.quote:
It
shows that the median bias hovered between $2 and $3 throughout our study period: it
grew from $2.2 in 2014 to $3.1 in 2016, then decreased to $2.5 in 2019, and grew again
to $2.8 in 2021. Meanwhile, policy bias in minimum wage laws also reﬂects an increasing
polarization in the US. The range of biases grew steadily from $2.7 in 2013 to $3.3 in
2016, $4.9 in 2019 and $6.1 in 2021. No state had a liberal bias in 2014, and the smallest
conservative bias was in Oregon at $1. By 2021, ten states had less conservative bias

than that, and three states (California, Washington, and DC) had a liberal policy bias.
decisions.reason: The shipped outcome quote ('we replicate and extend a recent such study (Simonovits, Guess, and Nagler, 2019)') only states the study's aim. The authors explicitly re-test whether the original conclusion of 'a pronounced and uniform conservative bias' has stood across 2014–2021, reporting a mixed result: on average across states, the pronounced conservative policy bias persisted ($2.2 to $3.1 median bias) alongside static responsiveness, but the uniform conservative bias across states no longer held by 2021, as over-responsive states closed the initial representation gap and three jurisdictions (California, Washington, and DC) shifted to a liberal policy bias.

decisions.quote:
We replicate and expand a recent study by Simonovits, Guess,

and Nagler (2019) to explore if its conclusion – a pronounced and uniform conservative

bias – has stood. Our analysis relies on seven national surveys ﬁelded between 2014

and 2021 that measure preferences about the minimum wage in U.S. dollars.
decisions.reason: Both shipped row 814 and blind coding agree that the record is a replication: the authors use new survey data fielded between 2014 and 2021 to re-test and extend the findings of Simonovits, Guess, and Nagler (2019).
